_comment: This tool's references, in citation order: the tool's pages number them [1], [2], ... in this order (IEEE style). Each needs an archived copy in the source-archive release, given as {"asset": "<file>"} and listed in sources/archive.json; never commit the file itself (see sources/README.md). Title style: 'quoted' for articles, web pages and parts of books; 'italic' for books, reports and datasets.

sources.pre: J. C. Pelland, J. F. Remmert, Z. P. Robinson, S. R. Hinson and M. C. Zourdos,
sources.title: The resistance training dose response: Meta-regressions exploring the effects of weekly volume and frequency on muscle hypertrophy and strength gains
sources.post: Sports Medicine, vol. 56, no. 2, pp. 481–505, 2026, doi: 10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w. Archived copy: preprint version 2 (the published article is not openly licensed, so it is not stored here), SportRχiv, Oct. 2024, doi: 10.51224/SRXIV.460.
sources.usedFor: Counting sets that train a muscle directly as 1 and indirectly as 0.5 (the 'fractional' method)

sources.pre: B. J. Schoenfeld, J. Grgic, C. Haun, T. Itagaki and E. R. Helms,
sources.title: Calculating set-volume for the limb muscles with the performance of multi-joint exercises: Implications for resistance training prescription
sources.usedFor: How much multi-joint exercises (presses, rows, squats) work the arm and leg muscles they don't mainly target

sources.title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e

sources.title: Hip thrust and back squat training elicit similar gluteus muscle hypertrophy and transfer similarly to the deadlift
sources.post: Frontiers in Physiology, vol. 14, art. 1279170, Oct. 2023, doi: 10.3389/fphys.2023.1279170.
sources.usedFor: The hip thrust and back squat grew the gluteus maximus similarly; neither grew the hamstrings
